rite.prompt: Who is murdered in the Hiramic legend Hall retells?

signal:
HIRAMIC.NFO                                        HALL 1.3
================================================================
The Hiramic Legend
Manly P. Hall · 1928 · folio p.227 · ECHO CRAFT.SYM

THESIS
  The murdered master of Solomon's temple is a solar myth
  wearing a craftsman's apron. The lost word is a sun that
  sets and must be raised.

POINTS
  * Hiram of Tyre supplies the work; Chiram Abiff is the maker
  * Three ruffians demand the Master's word at the gates
  * Acacia marks the grave — the sprig that does not die
  * Jacques de Molay as a later Hiram
  * Astronomical Chiram: the sun killed in the three winter months

SEE ALSO  freemasonic  pyramid  sun  flowers
DEGREE    NEOPHYTE may read this screen
================================================================
translation:
Solomon wants a house for God. Hiram of Tyre sends cedar and a master craftsman, Chiram Abiff, who knows the word that makes a Master. Three ruffians meet him at the gates of the unfinished temple and kill him when he will not give it up. The body is buried, an acacia sprig marks the grave, the word is lost, and the craft has been looking for it ever since.

Hall refuses to leave this as lodge fan-fiction. He stacks it on the dying-god pattern from earlier chapters (Tammuz, Adonis, Osiris) and then on the year: the sun “murdered” by the three winter months, buried, raised. Jacques de Molay, last Grand Master of the Temple, is offered as a historical rhyme — another master struck down, another word driven underground.

The pineal-gland aside is Hall at his most 1920s Theosophical. Take or leave it. The usable claim is architectural: a temple whose master is missing is a body without its word. Masonry, in this reading, is a play about rebuilding a killed sun inside a person.

This is the board’s first real door. The Lost Word, when we write it, starts here.
